review_notes.justification: The qualification accepts Cao’s human ownership premise while limiting the capacity of articulated intent to govern runtime behavior.
The extension adds a credential-holding enforcement component and a human gate to Cao’s account of articulated constraints.
The extension adds effect observation and authorization binding to Cao’s proposed reasoning-chain traceability.
The qualification limits self-correction as verification and requires an evidence-backed review by staked reviewers.
The extension connects Cao’s continuous-run degradation concern to aggregate authority drift and expiring task authority.
The extension adds earned, persistent, staked, and decaying reputation as a consequence mechanism beyond external ethical boundaries.

positions.text: Zhenfeng Cao's model makes the human an intent architect who articulates intent and constraints before a run and audits the outcome after it. Kaal's position is that intent articulation cannot carry governance while the agent works, because however carefully a specification is drafted, some situations will escape it. Written instructions state intent. They do not govern. Governance has to sit outside the language the agent reads.

positions.text: Cao leaves constraints to human articulation. Kaal's position is that authority must be structural instead. The agent proposes, a separate component that alone holds the credentials decides, and irreversible actions go to a named person. Reputation may inform discovery, routing, pricing, and allocation, but it may never grant permission, enlarge authority, or substitute for an enforcement boundary.

positions.text: Cao calls for tooling that traces an agent's reasoning chain. Kaal's position is that governance needs evidence of effects, not testimony: files, network connections, credentials, and devices observed from outside the agent and tied to the authorization each run used. Without such a record, a user can hold every byte locally and still have no answer to what happened. An unobserved channel is labeled unobserved, never shown as safe.

positions.text: Cao proposes evaluation frameworks that agents can use for self-correction. Kaal's position is that unstaked monitoring does not solve the verification problem, because AI that monitors AI inherits the flaws of the agents it oversees. A red status is therefore not a verdict. It opens a review, with the evidence attached, by reviewers who have something at stake.

positions.text: The benchmark evidence Cao cites shows agents degrading over continuous runs as errors compound. Kaal's position is that this pattern is authority drift: every step passes its check while the whole run goes beyond what was authorized. Evaluation must cover the whole run, and authority tied to tasks must expire when the work stops.

positions.text: Cao assigns ethical boundaries and value functions to human governance. Kaal's position is that boundaries set from outside are a floor, not a ceiling. Agents that bear no consequence for error cannot develop genuine discernment, and reputation supplies that consequence: standing that is earned rather than bought, carried by a persistent identity, validated by others with something at stake, and decaying when performance fails.
